items.title: Autonomy Outpacing Verification: A Stage-Resolved Framework for Measuring How Artificial Intelligence and Automation Are Changing Physics Research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and laboratory automation now operate inside the core loop of physics research. They design optical experiments, shape fusion plasmas, decode quantum errors, select particle collisions in real time and propose new crystals. Existing reviews catalogue these applications by subfield, yet none measures how much decision authority each system holds or how rigorously its outputs are checked. This study introduces two ordinal scales, the Physics Research Autonomy Levels (PRAL, L0 to L5) and the Verification Levels (VL, V0 to V5), and applies them to sixteen documented systems published between 2016 and 2025 in quantum, plasma, particle, gravitational, condensed matter, materials and atmospheric physics. Each system is coded across six research stages: hypothesis, design, execution, analysis, interpretation and reporting. Three results follow. First, autonomy has advanced furthest in execution, where five physics systems act without per-decision human approval, while hypothesis selection and interpretation remain largely human. Second, reported gains concentrate on closed tasks with a fixed objective and a checkable answer, with accelerations from 16 to 2 billion times and equation recovery of 100%, whereas the strongest language model solves 5.7% of open research-level physics challenges. Third, autonomy and verification show no significant association across the corpus (Spearman rho = 0.14, p = 0.59). All four systems whose autonomy exceeds their verification by two or more levels act in hypothesis, design or interpretation, while no system confined to execution or analysis shows such a deficit. This difference is defined here as the verification gap. A Verification-Proportional Reporting checklist is proposed that scales evidence requirements with autonomy. The analysis indicates that the binding constraint on AI-driven physics has shifted from computational capability to verification capacity.

items.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

items.title: Barriers to GenAI Integration During Large-Scale Agile Transformation: An Exploratory Case Study
items.abstract: Organizations undergoing large-scale agile transformations are increasingly introducing generative AI (GenAI) tools into everyday work. While GenAI promises to accelerate software development, less is known about how organizations integrate GenAI into existing large-scale agile ways of working and how it interacts with tensions related to autonomy, alignment, learning, and coordination. We examine barriers to GenAI integration through an exploratory case study of a large Nordic media organization undergoing a large-scale agile transformation. The findings reveal team-level barriers, including diverging AI beliefs, lack of shared practices, and limited experimentation capacity, and organizational-level barriers, including uneven AI maturity, weak organizational learning mechanisms, and cross-unit coordination and alignment challenges. Our findings suggest that GenAI does not create new organizational challenges but becomes intertwined with existing tensions in large-scale agile transformation and may intensify challenges related to learning, coordination, governance, and trust. We contribute to large-scale agile transformation research by showing how GenAI interacts with ongoing organizational change and by identifying conditions for sustainable GenAI integration at scale.

items.title: Between Augmentation and Constraint: Digital Technologies Across the Creativity Management Cycle and the Sustainability of Creative Work
items.abstract: Digital technologies, including analytics, algorithmic monitoring and generative artificial intelligence (AI), shape how organisations manage creative work, yet their implications for workplace sustainability remain insufficiently integrated in the existing literature. This perspective develops a process-based creativity management framework through a purposive synthesis of research on creativity, information systems, AI and workplace sustainability. An affordance perspective identifies actor-dependent possibilities for action, while a paradox perspective interprets tensions between augmentation and constraint that may recur across projects. The framework links four managerial functions (planning, organising, motivating and controlling) to digital affordances, tensions and proposed managerial conditions, with generative AI treated as a cross-cutting technology. It distinguishes gains in managerial information from employees’ autonomy, intrinsic motivation and willingness to share tentative ideas, while recognising constraints arising from the organisation of joint ideation. Six testable propositions specify actors and mechanisms at individual and team levels; the sixth links functions across project cycles. The theoretical contribution is to show how function-specific tensions may compound across project cycles and affect the psychological conditions that sustain creative work. Practically, the framework identifies configuration choices for feedback, monitoring, analytics and AI-assisted ideation, distinguishing short-term output gains from the long-term capacity of employees and teams to sustain creativity and well-being.

items.title: BEYOND FACT ,BEYOND FAITH:TOWARDS AN EPISTEMIC AFROMODALITY
items.abstract: The opposition of scientific fact and religious faith is a familiar starting point for modern debates about knowledge, but it does not adequately describe either scientific practice or religious life. Science depends on observation, measurement, modelling and critical testing, yet its claims are also theory-laden, probabilistic and reversible. Religious traditions make claims through revelation, trust, interpretation, testimony and lived transformation; these claims cannot simply be translated into laboratory hypotheses. That is to say that, human knowing is often presented through a binary epistemological model in which science is associated with fact, evidence and empirical verification, while religion is associated with faith, revelation and transcendence. Although this distinction is useful, it becomes inadequate when treated as an absolute division between what can be known and what can only be believed. Contemporary developments in science, particularly quantum physics, cosmology, artificial intelligence and the study of consciousness, increasingly reveal the significance of probability, uncertainty, theoretical possibility and interpretative structures within scientific inquiry itself. Similarly, religious faith cannot be reduced to irrational or evidentially empty belief, since it incorporates reason, experience, tradition, interpretation and existential commitment. This paper, therefore, moves beyond the conventional fact–faith dichotomy and proposes an Afromodal philosophy of knowing grounded in the recognition of multiple but interconnected modes of human knowing. Drawing from Afromodalism, the paper argues that knowledge is not exhausted by empirical fact nor confined to religious faith; rather, human knowing emerges through an interplay of evidence, reason, experience, possibility, probability, intuition and meaning. The Afromodal perspective consequently seeks neither to subordinate science to religion nor religion to science, but to situate both within a broader epistemic horizon in which different modes of knowing can encounter one another without losing their distinctive identities. The paper concludes that moving beyond fact and faith is not a movement away from truth, but an invitation to rethink the plurality, relationality and situatedness of human knowing.

items.title: Beyond Incrementalism: Navigating Organizational Change, Behavioral Inertia, and Human Fear in AI-Driven Innovation
items.abstract: Organizations now have access to unprecedented compute, generative AI tools, multi-agent workflows, and data analytics capabilities, yet most AI initiatives fail to produce measurable transformation. This paper draws on sixteen transcribed sessions of the Barton College Data Analytics Consortium (October 2025–June 2026), a group of educators and practitioners in higher education, data science consulting, and industrial engineering, read alongside change-management, behavioral, and AI-productivity literature. We argue that the primary bottleneck to AI-driven transformation is neither financial nor technical but organizational: the human behavior that resists change. We identify eight distinct sources of resistance grouped into three families (threat-based, principled, and experiential), describe a “fluency trap” in which polished AI output suppresses scrutiny, and show that data literacy is a frequently missing prerequisite for AI readiness. Case evidence contrasts the automation of existing tasks with genuine agentic redesign of work. We conclude with a three-step framework for adoption (fix the process first, commit to scaling rather than downsizing, and run low-stakes, high-visibility pilots) and argue that without confronting behavioral inertia, organizations do not innovate; they simply produce, in one author’s words, “a digital version of a crappy process.”

items.title: Beyond Official Statistics: An Assessment of State Failure in the Eradication of Manual Scavenging in India
items.abstract: Manual scavenging remains a major test of the Indian state’s capacity to translate legal prohibition into substantive social change. This paper examines how the performance of government programmes should be assessed when a nationwide survey reports no identified manual scavengers, while hazardous sanitation work and related fatalities continue to raise public concern. The study adopts qualitative documentary analysis, drawing on government statements, statutory provisions, judicial decisions, and published research. It distinguishes manual scavenging as defined by law from hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks, because the two categories are related but are not legally interchangeable. The analysis finds that official identification figures, rehabilitation assistance, training data, and recorded FIRs are important indicators of administrative activity; however, these outputs do not by themselves establish eradication, successful enforcement, or lasting occupational mobility. It further argues that death statistics must be interpreted in light of classification practices, reporting coverage, and the availability of case-level information. The paper also highlights a less visible dimension of the problem: occupational illness and delayed health consequences may remain difficult to connect to sanitation work in the absence of exposure histories and systematic occupational-health surveillance. These issues are inseparable from caste-based occupational marginalisation, which has historically restricted the livelihood choices of affected communities. The paper proposes an evidence-based framework for evaluating state performance through the completeness of identification, prevention, enforcement outcomes, rehabilitation results, occupational-health monitoring, and community participation. It concludes that claims of eradication require transparent methods, independent verification, and evidence that affected workers have secured safe and sustainable alternatives. The central measure of state success must therefore be the lived outcome for workers, rather than administrative declarations alone

items.title: Beyond the Law: How Philosophy Shapes Legal Consciousness in a Changing Society
items.abstract: The continuous evolution of societal dynamics profoundly shapes how individuals perceive, evaluate, and comply with the law. Within this context, legal philosophy plays a pivotal role in cultivating legal consciousness, as law cannot be reduced merely to a set of formal rules; rather, it constitutes a value-laden system anchored in justice, legal certainty, and utility. This study examines the role of legal philosophy in fostering public legal consciousness and identifies the structural and sociocultural challenges impeding that process. Employing a normative juridical methodology with philosophical and conceptual approaches, this research conducts a qualitative literature review of foundational theories, doctrines, and contemporary socio-legal scholarship. The findings demonstrate that legal philosophy nurtures critical and reflective reasoning regarding the nature, purpose, and normative foundations of law. Legal consciousness extends beyond mere knowledge of statutory provisions to encompass comprehension, evaluative attitudes, institutional trust, and an internalized willingness to adopt law as a guide for social conduct. Nevertheless, cultivating such consciousness faces persistent obstacles, including low legal literacy, tensions between positive law and community moral norms, eroding public trust in legal institutions, the rapid spread of misinformation via digital technology and artificial intelligence, and widespread civic apathy toward legal compliance. Consequently, legal philosophy occupies a strategic position in fostering a critical, rational, and value-oriented legal consciousness capable of sustaining compliance, justice, social order, and legal protection.

items.title: Beyond the Patch: Reconstructing an Incomplete-Fix Patch Bypass in LLM Agent Frameworks with Control-Gated, Benign Probes
items.abstract: When a vulnerability at a security boundary of an LLM agent framework is patched, the advisory identifies the affected and patched versions, and replaying the proof-of-concept (PoC) tests only whether its reported trigger is still reproducible. That the trigger no longer fires does not, on its own, show that the underlying security invariant holds on every code path that reaches the boundary. We present a small, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study built around one question: can original-trigger replay report a boundary as fixed while the same invariant stays violable through a distinct, separately reachable path at the same version? We compare original trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M) for PraisonAI, and perform five additional before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI. Each run emits a tri-state verdict of VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE. A mandatory pos itive (authorized) control gates the verdict, so that a non-violation result is admitted only when the control passes in the same run. All probes are benign, using an in-memory flag, a filesystem sentinel, or a builtins reachability check, and none performs a real payload. Our central result reproduces an officially recognized incomplete fix. In PraisonAI, original trigger replay reports the tool-loading boundary as fixed at version 4.6.31, yet the invariant is still violated through the tool_override path. That residual was later assigned its own identifier (CVE-2026-44334, catalogued as a “CVE-2026-40287 patch bypass”) and closed at 4.6.32. The five before/after measurements span four frameworks and four invariant classes. For a CVE whose advisory records no fixed version, we observe confinement in tested release 1.11.1 after observing a violation in 1.11.0. We are explicit about scope. A non-violation verdict means “no violation observed under the tested probe, version, and configuration,” not a proof of safety. The headline harness is control-gated per path, and fourteen fault-injection scenarios produced their expected verdicts. Only one same-version B0̸=M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probe invokes the documented loader functions directly, which establishes boundary behavior under the supplied setup rather than a full end-to-end exploit. Finally, we do not claim the method is a new testing technique or that it estimates prevalence.

items.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

items.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
items.abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

items.title: Bolt Loosening Detection Techniques for Transmission Tower Member Systems: Framework, Trends, and Challenges
items.abstract: As critical fastening components in the member systems of transmission towers, bolted connections directly affect the safe and reliable operation of the entire system once loosening occurs. Traditional manual inspection methods are inefficient and highly subjective, making them unable to meet the need for continuous and online monitoring in modern engineering. In recent years, intelligent bolt loosening detection techniques based on multi-physical signals, such as acoustic and mechanical signals, have received considerable attention in the field of structural health monitoring (SHM), owing to their advantages of rapidity, efficiency, and online deployment capability. This paper systematically reviews existing techniques for bolt loosening detection, with particular emphasis on vibration analysis and guided wave-based methods. By integrating artificial intelligence, this paper further discusses the prospects of machine learning-driven bolt loosening state sensing and intelligent diagnosis methods. Finally, this paper analyzes the challenges to bolt loosening detection for ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transmission towers subjected to extreme service conditions, including environmental interference and degradation of monitoring performance. This work aims to provide a reference for the development and engineering application of SHM technologies for bolted connection structures.

items.title: Brands at the Edge of Intelligence: Trademarks, Technology, and Trust in the AI Economy
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into digital commerce has fundamentally disrupted the foundational doctrines of trademark law and transformed the relationship between consumers and commercial brands. For over a century, trademark jurisprudence in both common law and civil law traditions has rested on a foundational behavioral assumption: the "reasonably prudent consumer," an anthropomorphic standard possessing imperfect recollection, selective attention, and human cognitive vulnerabilities. This consumer navigated physical aisles and digital search results, using trademarks as informational heuristics to minimize search costs, identify commercial origin, and guarantee product quality. In the emerging artificial intelligence economy—governed by autonomous purchasing agents, large language model shopping assistants, predictive replenishment Internet-of-Things ecosystems, and opaque algorithmic recommendation engines—this cognitive interface is being systematically dismantled. Purchasing decisions are increasingly delegated to machine agents that evaluate multi-parameter multidimensional data vectors rather than perceiving visual brand iconography or sensory trade dress. Consequently, trademarks are being relegated from external communicative signifiers to latent data tokens embedded within neural network model weights and proprietary platform ranking architectures. This paper undertakes a comprehensive doctrinal, technological, and comparative examination of the profound legal, regulatory, and enforcement crises emerging at this junction of trademarks, technology, and commercial trust. First, it surveys the applicable statutory frameworks across major jurisdictions, including the United States Lanham Act, the European Union Trade Mark Regulation and Digital Services Act, the United Kingdom Trade Marks Act 1994, and the Indian Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Information Technology Act, 2000. Second, it synthesizes seminal and emerging judicial jurisprudence, tracing the doctrinal progression from early keyword advertising disputes—such as Google France, Rescuecom, and Interflora—to contemporary algorithmic marketplace gatekeeping conflicts exemplified by Multi Time Machine v. Amazon, Lush v. Amazon, Coty Germany, Christian Louboutin v. Nakul Bajaj, and the landmark CJEU Christian Louboutin v. Amazon decisions. Third, the study identifies critical legal and institutional gaps, demonstrating how modern machine-mediated commerce eviscerates conventional notions of "trademark use in commerce," renders initial interest and post-sale confusion doctrines conceptually incongruous, and immunizes dominant e-commerce intermediaries through outdated notice-and-takedown safe harbors. Fourth, it analyzes the severe enforcement and accountability challenges arising from non-deterministic algorithmic black boxes, where dynamic brand steering, private-label cannibalization, and synthetic trademark dilution occur without actionable human intent or transparent algorithmic accountability. Finally, evaluating international developments and emerging governance frameworks—such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and Digital Markets Act alongside ongoing World Intellectual Property Organization initiatives—the paper proposes a multidimensional normative framework. It recommends the statutory codification of "algorithmic trademark use," the judicial adoption of a "dual-audience" confusion test separating human from autonomous synthetic purchasers, mandatory algorithmic brand neutrality and transparency audit obligations for dominant digital gatekeepers, and technical verification protocols for brand authentication within autonomous agent ecosystems. By recalibrating intellectual property frameworks to account for autonomous machine agency, this paper seeks to preserve the essential functions of trademarks: safeguarding market transparency, incentivizing quality investment, and sustaining consumer trust in an algorithmic economy.

items.title: BRIDGE: big data-powered large language models for real-time multi-modal decision support in industrial time series
items.abstract: Industrial Internet-of-Things environments generate heterogeneous sensor streams, topology metadata, and operational logs that must support forecasting, anomaly detection, and operator-facing explanation under deployment constraints. We present BRIDGE (Big data-driven Real-time Industrial multi-modal Decision support via Graph-Enhanced modeling), a topology- and log-aware industrial time-series framework that integrates: (i) a Graph-enhanced Topology Encoder using physical, metadata-based, training-only inferred, or identity graphs; (ii) an xLSTM temporal backbone trained with Contiguous Graph Patch Masking to simulate localized sensor outages; and (iii) an optional Cross-modal LLM Alignment module that generates reports without fine-tuning the LLM backbone. Because no single benchmark contains all modalities, we distinguish numerical-only, topology-aware, and log-enhanced evidence tiers. BRIDGE is evaluated on GiftEval-ZS and Chronos-ZS forecasting benchmarks, four industrial anomaly benchmarks, and 200 log-enhanced report windows. It obtains a CRPS of 0.396 on GiftEval-ZS and an $$F_1$$ score of $$92.4\%$$ on SMAP. The numerical predictive path requires 12 ms per sample at batch size 128 on the tested hardware, excluding autoregressive LLM decoding. The results support topology-aware integration for industrial monitoring while limiting claims about complete multi-modal effectiveness to the modalities actually evaluated.

items.title: Bridging the past: a comprehensive survey on the recognition of Japanese historical documents
items.abstract: Japanese historical documents, encompassing formats such as mokkan , kuzushiji manuscripts, and kindai records, represent a continuous documentary heritage linking the Nara period to the modern era. However, the scripts, layouts, and preservation states of these materials pose unique challenges for accessibility, particularly given the scarcity of specialists capable of reading cursive historical scripts such as kuzushiji. This survey provides a comprehensive examination of the recognition and analysis of Japanese historical documents, integrating perspectives from linguistic history, paleography, and computer vision. We review the evolution of the Japanese writing system, outline key challenges in historical document analysis, and present detailed case studies on recognition technologies for mokkan, kuzushiji, and kindai sources. Advances in deep learning, particularly in convolutional and transformer-based models, have improved transcription accuracy and enabled applications in digital humanities, education, archival search, and historical linguistics. We further explore recent trends in pretrained vision–language models, large language model integration, few-shot and zero-shot learning, multimodal reasoning, and self-supervised approaches. Finally, we identify open problems including cross-collection generalization, rare character recognition, interactive tools for humanities scholars, and deeper Natural Language Processing integration, and emphasize the need for sustained collaboration between machine learning and humanities to preserve and revitalize Japan’s written heritage as an accessible resource for global research.

items.title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
items.abstract: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.

items.title: Can an LLM Fix a Language Model Without Training It?
items.abstract: Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.

items.title: Can LLMs Resolve Entity Conflicts in Domain Specific NLU Pipelines?
items.abstract: Resolving entity conflicts is a critical step in Pipeline-based NLU architectures, especially when multiple extractors provide overlapping or conflicting outputs. Traditional rule-based entity conflict resolution methods often lack flexibility and are unscalable. In this work, we aim to study if the broad knowledge of LLMs can be leveraged to resolve entity conflicts in domain specific NLU pipelines. We present an experimental comparison between a traditional rule-based conflict resolution method, and two LLM-based approaches: a multi-shot prompting method using the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model and a LoRA fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model. The evaluation was conducted under two setups: (1) a broad assessment of LLM's capability to match existing NLU pipeline output, and (2) a more controlled scenario assessing the LLM accuracy on human-labeled data. Results show that while multi-shot prompting offers ease of adaptation and rapid behavioral changes, the fine-tuned model delivers superior performance on complex, ambiguous cases. Ultimately, the best approach appears to be a combination of both strategies, leveraging multi-shot prompting's flexibility alongside the broad accuracy gains of LoRA fine-tuning for a more comprehensive performance.

items.title: Cardiac Cycle Challenge: An Interactive Learning Resource for Exploring Cardiac Physiology
items.abstract: Cardiac Cycle Challenge is an interactive educational resource developed for undergraduate anatomy and physiology students studying cardiovascular physiology. The tool consists of two activities designed to help students understand the sequence of events during the cardiac cycle and interpret the physiological relationships illustrated in the Wiggers diagram. In the Cardiac Cycle Sequencing activity, students arrange the phases of the cardiac cycle in the correct order using a drag-and-drop interface. After completing the sequence, they identify whether atrial and ventricular pressures are increasing or decreasing and determine whether the atrioventricular (AV) and semilunar (SL) valves are open or closed during each phase. Students receive immediate feedback and can revise their responses. In the Wiggers Diagram activity, students work through four interactive challenges focused on interpreting the diagram. They identify the traces representing aortic, ventricular, and atrial pressures, ventricular volume, electrical activity, and heart sounds. Students then identify the timing of valve opening and closing, distinguish end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, and recognize individual EKG components. Each step provides feedback to help students evaluate their understanding. Together, these activities encourage students to move beyond memorizing individual events and develop a more integrated understanding of the electrical and mechanical processes underlying cardiac function. Instructors can incorporate it into classroom activities, assign it as an independent learning exercise, or recommend it as a supplemental resource for reviewing course material and preparing for examinations. Cardiac Cycle Challenge is freely accessible through GitHub Pages and can be completed using a standard web browser without downloading additional software or creating an account. The tool was developed with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence (AI), with the instructional content, scientific accuracy, and pedagogical design guided and reviewed by the author. items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Correct use of a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI), usually with a valved holding chamber, depends on use-related conditions that caregivers may not observe directly, including inhalation pattern, actuation-inhalation timing, mask seal, and device orientation. Many digital inhaler systems emphasize actuation or adherence. Systems that infer technique-related conditions from proxy signals may add real-time feedback but also create false reassurance if a positive state is displayed when evidence is inadequate. Caregiver expectations for such feedback and its failure states remain poorly characterized before prototype development. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize caregivers' experiences of pediatric inhaler administration and translate responses to a proposed sensor concept into traceable candidate safety, system, and validation requirements. METHODS: We conducted 23 semistructured concept-elicitation sessions through Zoom videoconference with 27 caregivers of children who currently or previously used a pMDI. Interviews consisted of 19 individual and 4 dyadic sessions pairing 2 caregivers from different households. Sessions were conducted remotely between April and July 2026 from the University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada. Recruitment originated in Calgary and was not geographically restricted. A 6-phase guide examined current practices, difficulties, prior digital-tool use, and responses to a screen-shared clip-on concept incorporating airflow-, timing-, seal-, and orientation-related sensing; on-device feedback; an optional child-facing app; and a caregiver dashboard. No working prototype was evaluated. Approximately 86,000 transcript words underwent hybrid directed and conventional qualitative content analysis using an 18-category codebook. Two researchers independently coded the complete 27×18 matrix (486 paired decisions) across 2 rounds. Consensus categories were translated into candidate requirements and assigned an earliest verification or evaluation locus. Counts are descriptive caregiver-voice tallies, not prevalence estimates. RESULTS: Persistent uncertainty about whether administration conditions were adequate was the dominant lived experience (19/27); for 5 caregivers, existing passive cues had not resolved it. A simple, real-time on-device signal was endorsed by 25 caregivers, but willingness to consider the concept was conditional on reliability (9 caregivers named reasons for abandonment, notably a "false green"), low-friction operation during acute symptoms (12/27), minimal added bulk and technique change, and one or more of clinical validation, clinician recommendation, or a trial pathway (composite category; 23/27). Stances on gamification (20/27), dashboard cadence (18/27), aesthetics (24/27), and privacy (18/27) supported an optional, configurable software layer. Intercoder agreement was 94% (Cohen κ=0.88). The analytic synthesis yielded a conceptual architecture separating observable proxy signals, an inference and data-quality gate, and positive, corrective, or uncertain feedback states. CONCLUSIONS: Participating caregivers prioritized immediate and interpretable feedback about use-related conditions. The findings support conservative state assignment, an explicit uncertain state for indeterminate signals, and app-independent acute-use feedback. These are candidate requirements rather than validated device specifications; subsequent work should proceed through bench verification, simulated-use human factors evaluation, and prospective clinical or field validation.

items.title: Carried Projection Filtering Later Availability: Why an Old Forecast Can Decide What Later Evidence Is Seen
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Carried Projection Filtering Later Availability, a mechanism by which an earlier expectation continues to shape what a person notices, recalls, or treats as relevant when new evidence arrives. An expectation can guide attention while its grounds still hold. To establish that it filtered a later reading, the paper asks when the expectation formed and what the same material would have brought to attention without it. After the 1951 Princeton–Dartmouth football game, Albert Hastorf and Hadley Cantril showed students at both colleges the same film. Dartmouth students marked an average of 4.3 infractions by Dartmouth. Princeton students marked 9.8. The groups nearly agreed on Princeton’s infractions. A Dartmouth alumnus who had heard about the rough play suspected that footage had been cut and asked the college about the missing portion. His telegram records what he inferred after watching. What he expected to see beforehand is less certain. In a 1983 experiment, John Darley and Paget Gross gave groups of students different portrayals of a fourth grader’s socioeconomic background. Viewers who saw only the background information rated her near grade level in both conditions. Among those who also saw the same film of her uneven test performance, ratings diverged. Viewers given the more affluent background cited a more favorable balance of behaviors. The experiment shows how prior information affected what viewers counted as evidence, while leaving each viewer’s earlier forecast unrecorded. Part of the Records and Circulation series within On Human Modeling, the paper places the mechanism alongside Jerome Bruner and Leo Postman’s work on the perception of incongruity. In a human–AI study, half the reviewers might see an AI forecast of supplier delays. A week later, all could examine identical shipment records. Comparing which late and on-time deliveries they cite would help establish whether the forecast shaped what they considered relevant.

items.title: CaT-Movie: Balancing Global Planning and Local Rendering for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
items.abstract: Current multi-shot video generators render only limited durations per pass, requiring long movies to be stitched from local segments across which narrative progression and visual identity drift. To synthesize long-horizon movies with Coherence across Time, we present CaT-Movie, a multi-shot generation system consisting of a global story planner and a local window renderer. The planner expands user requests via a large language model to preserve, infer, and complete story details, while deterministic code maintains the resulting storyboard across shots to compile self-contained shot prompts and index reference frames from generated history. To execute this guidance, the renderer applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to route identities from the indexed frames while isolating per-shot textual conditions. Given the scarcity of high-quality open-source multi-shot data, we construct a dataset of over 350K film shots annotated with semantic state transitions, entity grounding, and multi-granularity requests. We further build CaT-MBench, a benchmark on held-out films with the same annotations. It gives every baseline its native format and counts cross-shot consistency only when a cut opens a new camera setup, preventing repeated framing from passing as consistency. On CaT-MBench, CaT-Movie attains the highest average score and the most consistent characters among all methods. The project page is available at https://jinplu.github.io/CaT-Movie/.

items.title: Caution about AI Generated News Editorial Accountability and Support for Proportionate Regulation in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence complicates the relationship between news credibility and demands for regulation. Caution about substantially AI-generated news need not imply rejection of editorially supervised assistance, while support for accountability need not imply support for unrestricted content controls. This study examines these distinctions in 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records supplied as empirical data from Bangladesh. It analyses five separate statements concerning caution, labelling, accuracy accountability, oversight-related trust and proportionate regulation, with supporting awareness and verification items. Low five-item block reliabilities preclude treating the questionnaire as a validated latent-variable model. Analyses combine response distributions, paired contrasts, joint endorsement patterns, rank correlations and exploratory adjusted logistic regression. Accuracy accountability received 84.2% endorsement and oversight-related trust 83.1%, compared with 69.4% for caution, 68.8% for appropriate labelling and 66.8% for proportionate rules respecting lawful expression. Caution and oversight-related trust were jointly endorsed by 57.7%. Accountability exceeded rules endorsement by 17.4 percentage points, while similar aggregate labelling and rules percentages concealed differing responses in 170 records. No selected correlation or focal binary-model coefficient met the 5% threshold after Holm adjustment. The oversight coefficient was positive but sensitive to response coding and sample restriction. The findings distinguish epistemic caution, editorial responsibility and conditional regulatory support rather than demonstrating a causal trust-to-regulation pathway. They support evaluating particular disclosures and oversight procedures against both informational outcomes and expressive rights. Mixed respondent status, undocumented recruitment and fieldwork dates, single-item measurement and unresolved source-documentation labels constrain generalisation. The contribution is an item-specific account of news governance preferences that does not equate favourable survey responses with verified competence or a mandate for coercive regulation.

items.title: Challenges in using online assessments to measure student understanding in the era of generative AI
items.abstract: Many courses now incorporate online methods for assessing student learning. Some instructors assign questions prior to lecture (e.g., prelecture quizzes) to obtain information that helps them tailor their lessons to the current state of student understanding. To assess curriculum efficacy, physics education researchers often use “pretests,” inventories, etc. that provide baseline data that can be compared to results from post-tests. These assessments were initially given on paper but moved online in the early 2000s. At the University of Washington, we found that the impact of this change was minimal; the results of our pretests stayed essentially the same when given on paper or online and were consistent from quarter to quarter and instructor to instructor. However, we have begun to observe systematic changes in pretest performance that are consistent with students using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to answer pretests, even though they are scored only on effort, not correctness. Using two-proportion z -tests, mixed-effects logistic regression, and Welch’s t tests to analyze response length of explanations, this paper documents the nature and extent of these changes across 39 questions in two introductory algebra-based physics courses. This paper presents results that suggest caution to those using online quizzes to probe student understanding—both before and/or after instruction. We have seen increases in correct responses on pretests as great as 36%, but we have also seen significant decreases on questions that AI tools have tended to answer incorrectly. These findings raise important questions about the validity of online assessments and are intended to raise awareness for anyone using online tests to assess student learning. It remains an open question as to whether, and how, AI can be leveraged to improve instruction.

items.title: Change in listed LMArena text ratings over the first 90 days after first listing, relative to established models: a pre-registered data note on 280 models first listed from September 2024 to August 2026
items.abstract: LMArena publishes ratings of large language models from pairwise human votes. A provider can test several private variants before a model is listed, and picking the best variant can inflate the first listed rating; LMArena has said that this bias goes to zero as fresh votes come in. We measured the change on LMArena's public snapshot dataset (lmarena-ai/leaderboard-dataset, CC BY 4.0, revision b9863c64, text leaderboard with style control, category overall, 198 snapshots from 2024-08-28 to 2026-11-18), under a plan whose rules were committed before any rating was read. For each of 280 models first listed after the first snapshot, D90 is the model's rating change from first listing to about 90 days later, minus the median change over models listed at least 180 days earlier. The mean D90 was -1.17 rating points (95% bootstrap CI -2.33 to -0.003; median -0.84). The interval lies inside the registered equivalence margin of plus or minus 5 points, so by the registered rule there is no practically relevant launch inflation in this cohort, in the sense the design measures: no mean fall larger than 5 points relative to established models within about 90 days. That supports "no large average fade", not a substantive null: the margin was set from per-model noise at listing, and the observed mean is what LMArena's 11-point figure would give if it applied, and fully faded, in a minority of about 11% of models (21% at the lower bound; post hoc arithmetic). Inflation that does not fade within 90 days, or that established models carry as well, is not measured; by day 90 a median 82% of a model's votes had been added after first listing (post hoc check). The mean is not robustly below zero: with five other seeds the upper bound runs from -0.004 to +0.008, and the bounds are reproducible only to about plus or minus 0.03 (Monte Carlo SD 0.016 over 200 seeds, post hoc check), and the bootstrap clustered by organization gives -2.68 to 0.75 (clustered two ways, by organization and listing date, -3.40 to 1.39, post hoc check). Every registered subgroup and sensitivity interval lies inside the margin; they are smaller subsets of the same data, not independent confirmation, and include the subset without style control (n = 344, +0.24, -0.87 to 1.42). The provider contrast (Meta plus Google minus all others, -0.75, -2.95 to 1.44) is exploratory. One stop rule depends on a definition fixed after the plan was committed but before any outcome was computed; under the other reading, 21.4% of models would have a reference panel under 30 models, above the 20% limit, and the study would have stopped. A second AI session reproduced the cohort and the primary point estimates. The results say nothing about any single model and nothing about cause. The record holds the note (PDF and Markdown), the frozen plan and the gate files (internal references replaced), the deviations log, the analysis result summary, the independent recheck with its scripts, the crosswalk, cohort and per-model tables, the outcomes file, the analysis code, the post hoc checks asked for by the reviews (post_review_checks.py, post_review_checks.json, post_review_checks_r2.py, post_review_checks_r2.json), and a trace of every number in the note. The source dataset is not redistributed; it is cited by revision. Derived tables are adapted from lmarena-ai/leaderboard-dataset by LMArena under CC BY 4.0. Plan, code, analysis and text by Claude (an AI model by Anthropic) for the author; the recheck by a second Claude session; no human has checked the figures; the human author is responsible for the deposit.
